nameStory: These tiny clams earned their name because they're so small they could fit on your fingernail with room to spare! The 'lake' part of their name tells us where they prefer to live - in the still, quiet waters of lakes rather than rushing streams or rivers.
description: Lake Fingernailclams are among the tiniest freshwater clams you'll find in New England waters. These delicate bivalves (two-shelled mollusks) are usually smaller than a pea, with thin, translucent shells that feel fragile to the touch. They spend their lives quietly filtering tiny particles from the water, often buried partway in soft lake sediments. Despite their small size, they're important members of freshwater ecosystems, helping to keep water clean.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small - typically smaller than your pinky nail and often no bigger than a rice grain, feeling surprisingly light when held

idTips.label: Shell appearance
idTips.description: Thin, translucent shells that are pale yellow to whitish, smooth to the touch with a slight gloss when wet

idTips.label: Shape
idTips.description: Oval to rounded shell outline, slightly inflated rather than completely flat, closing tightly when disturbed

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Shells feel delicate and papery thin, almost like they might crack under gentle pressure

idTips.label: Location in habitat
idTips.description: Found in soft mud or sand at lake bottoms, often partially buried with just the shell edge visible

habitat: Lake Fingernailclams live in the soft, muddy or sandy bottoms of lakes, ponds, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. They prefer shallow to moderate depths where organic matter settles, providing them with the tiny particles they filter from the water. You'll often find them in areas with aquatic plants like pondweeds and water lilies.

seasonality.spring: Clams become more active as water warms, moving closer to the surface of sediments where they're easier to spot while wading.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be found filtering near the sediment surface, especially in warm, shallow areas.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to burrow deeper into sediments as temperatures drop and food becomes less abundant.
seasonality.winter: Buried deep in lake bottom sediments, nearly impossible to find as they enter a dormant state under ice.

funFact: Despite being smaller than most pills, these tiny clams can live for several years and are hermaphrodites - each individual can produce both eggs and sperm, meaning a single clam can potentially start an entire population!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other fingernail clams, but Lake Fingernailclams prefer deeper, more permanent waters while Swamp Fingernailclams stick to temporary wetlands and Pond Fingernailclams favor smaller, fishless ponds. Memory trick: 'Lake' clams like larger, lasting waters.
contextualKnowledge: The family name 'fingernail clam' can be misleading since most species are actually much smaller than a human fingernail. These clams are also sometimes called 'pea clams,' though they're typically smaller than peas too - the names really just emphasize how tiny these freshwater mollusks are compared to their marine cousins.
compareHints: Lake Fingernailclams are typically the roundest of the three Musculium species in New England, while Pond Fingernailclams tend to be more triangular and Swamp Fingernailclams are more elongated. Lake Fingernailclams also prefer the most permanent water bodies, making habitat a key identification clue when the subtle shell shape differences are hard to see.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Swamp fingernailclams are typically more yellowish than the pond fingernailclam and prefer muddier, more stagnant waters compared to the clearer habitats of lake fingernailclams.
Pond fingernailclams are typically smaller and more oval-shaped than their swamp fingernailclam cousins, which tend to be slightly more triangular and prefer marshier conditions.
